prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry in Romanian that makes memory, the body and dream into an expansive imaginative cosmology.

statement.case_for: My first preference is unchanged after the exchange. On the common criteria, the claim for Cărtărescu rests on an unmistakable voice, a formal architecture that can be judged across forms and decades, and an imaginative and intellectual depth that sits in how the works are built. Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid, as publicly known, make memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation into one system, and the poetry and essays appear to belong to the same project. The case does not rest on nationality, fame or political symbolism. The chair asked what would change my first preference. A demonstrated pattern in which the late long novels recycle the motifs and structures of the earlier ones without adding new formal work would move me, and I would then move toward Adonis. So would a reliable reading showing that the sentence-level texture is much thinner than the architecture suggests. I should also state a refinement. My fourth place for Adonis in the opening ranking mainly reflects lower evidentiary confidence, because I cannot judge Arabic prosody. It is not a finding that the achievement is lesser. I think his case is of the same rank as the leading candidate, and I hold it in reserve as my first alternative.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that my judgment rests on public knowledge and translation, not on direct reading or independent verification. The very long, recursive late books may contain excess or repetition that I cannot rule out. The poetry, early prose and essays are thinly covered in translation, so a citation naming prose and poetry together leans mostly on the major novels. Someone could fairly say that this is a narrower evidential base than 'whole oeuvre' implies. A second weakness is that I have been asking for Arabic-language verification of Adonis while accepting a lighter standard for Romanian prose. The architecture of a novel is more testable in translation than a prosodic innovation, but that difference is one of degree. If the committee applies a common standard, as Carlberg and Mattson suggest, my own case also needs a Romanian-language reading. If no such reading can be obtained, the Adonis claim of changing a poetic language may deserve more weight than I give it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first and argues that building a personal cosmos in prose and changing the language of a poetic tradition are different kinds of achievement, and that the first is not obviously the greater. He says the translation uncertainty should affect how carefully we read and not how much we trust the candidate, and he asks whether Cărtărescu's poetry and essays strengthen that case.
responses.response: I accept the first point and have said that Adonis's achievement may be a larger kind if verified. I also accept the second in part. Translation loss applies to all poetry, and I should not let it quietly lower a poet's standing. Still, I think the question of how much a committee can confirm is a legitimate part of its judgment, provided it says so openly. On his question, I have to be candid. I know Cărtărescu's poetry and essays least, and I cannot honestly say they strengthen the case. The case rests mostly on the prose. For that reason my citation names poetry as part of a unified project but does not make it the basis. I would not want that wording to claim more than the committee can support.

responses.point: Carlberg keeps Adonis first and says she would move Cărtărescu to first if the quality of the long novels holds across the whole body. She also reads my own position as resting on public knowledge and accepts the caution about judging Arabic poetry in translation.
responses.response: Her condition is the right test, and it is close to mine in reverse. We both name the late long novels as the pivot, so a close reading of them would decide more than any further argument about influence or reputation. I would count it as evidence of extension if the later books add a new structural principle, as the shortlist's description of Solenoid suggests. I would count it as evidence of repetition if they replay the earlier motifs on a larger scale without new form. I cannot say which it is from public knowledge. I agree with her that any political or cultural standing of a candidate should be kept out of the assessment, and I would apply that to Wright and Zurita as well as Adonis.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis second. He words his citation around remaking the novel on a large scale, and he says that if the late books proved diluted he would look again at Adonis.
responses.response: I share his conditional and would take the same step, from Cărtărescu to Adonis. On wording, I prefer not to centre the citation on 'remaking the novel'. That phrase makes a historical claim about the genre that I cannot verify. I would rather describe what the books do: they build memory, the body and dream into a cumulative cosmology. Naming prose and poetry together stays closer to the single project we all describe. I would accept his narrower wording if the other supporters preferred it, because the difference is one of emphasis and not of the writer credited.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first. She holds that the major prose works keep their structure better in translation than a prosodic innovation would, and that Adonis's achievement is hard to separate from his reputation without the originals.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction between architecture and prosody, and it is the basis of my own confidence ranking. I would add one limit. A structure that survives translation is easier to see, but being easier to see does not make it greater. I try not to let testability decide the comparison alone. Her point that the committee should ask for readings of the originals for both writers is one I support. I also note that her second place for Wright and my third place show only a partial overlap in our secondary preferences, and I would not want that read as agreement about the strength of Wright's case. I still hold that a small number of large novels is a thinner basis for a whole-oeuvre citation.

uncertainties: I have not read the work directly. My assessment of Cărtărescu rests on general public knowledge, and I cannot verify how much of the Romanian verbal texture survives in translation.
Whether the very long late books extend the project or repeat it is unresolved and unverified, and it is the main condition that could change my first preference.
The poetry, early prose and essays are thinly covered in translation, so a whole-oeuvre citation leans mostly on the major novels.

My lower ranking of Adonis reflects evidentiary confidence about Arabic prosody and not an established judgment of merit. Under common standards of verification the two cases may be closer than my opening ranking suggests, and I cannot settle this without readings of the Arabic.

For the other shortlisted writers, including Carson, Wright, Can Xue, Michon, NDiaye and Zurita, I cannot independently judge the original-language prose or verse. Questions about the weight of scholarship, translation and non-textual projects in the Carson and Zurita cases remain open.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which shows no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own fiction and my work on Selma Lagerlöf are context only and are not treated as evidence for or against any candidate. My Nobel Prize Museum interview in 2024 was given for the committee and says nothing about the 2026 shortlist. My simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the full Swedish Academy makes the actual decision.
